caption:
A Chinese-speaking hacker used AI agents to break into the websites of more than 100 companies, including Deere, SharkNinja and Cummins, Reuters reports.
The agents tried over 1,200 sites. Each successful break-in took about 23 hours and roughly $50 in AI tokens, a researcher estimates.

Should open source AI hacking tools be locked down?

Follow @neurafeed.ai for daily AI news.

Source: Reuters

slides.headline: One hacker let AI agents break into *100+ company websites*. Each hack cost about $50

slides.heading: Deere, SharkNinja and *Cummins* hit
paras: A Chinese-speaking hacker used AI agents to break into the websites of more than 100 companies, Reuters reports. Named victims include Deere, SharkNinja and Cummins.
Deere says it saw no sign sensitive information was accessed. SharkNinja says only a standalone support site was hit and the threat was contained.

slides.heading: Orders in under *100 characters*
paras: The attacker used Cairn, an open source platform that takes a target and a goal and sets AI agents to work on it step by step.
The instructions were fewer than 100 Chinese characters: find a way to run code on each site, then plant an uploader web shell. The agents did the rest.

slides.heading: *$50* and 23 hours per break-in
paras: Since September 25, the agents tried more than 1,200 sites, mostly online shops in the US, Canada, Australia and Japan. A successful intrusion took about 23 hours.
Researcher Snorre Fagerland of NorForge estimates about $5,000 in AI tokens in total, roughly $50 for each successful hack.

slides.heading: Claude Code and *DeepSeek*?
paras: Every task ran on a worker named claudecode_deepseek-v4.1-flash. NorForge reads that as Claude Code running DeepSeek's low cost V4.1 Flash model.

paras.t: "It's not script kiddie stuff," Fagerland told Reuters.

slides.note: Cairn's author says the platform was not designed for hacking.

slides.hook: AI agents are making hacking cheap and fast. Follow to hear about the next attack before it reaches you.
